``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("84a6ccaaab1596139d28e822f40cc99c68d337d4c81d1c6d9692c1d6bb22e4af", "6044974c633b3a319c31bb32110411520c425e89722a64806528553227e7a50a", "0910ecfa049738ef3f2540855341a380df89224ff71da94b4c21689fd66f62e3", "b8b81af76163bdcc5b4f7d8fe6795f164991f8a62678c971db031b9e90a27813", "ef9a1896eeaae929800eade768276e2240ef252d26d0d96c1950a1a5e1aadb34", "e5d8350f1540fe91145dc262c455bca7748ad97dafb2d9facd5adebed9f66d2d", "41957bd0ba2d9c07af2e069f10780fdf6b2102c065bebe0db2136dfe07d67a28", "33b58598eb317553942e27545982d4c25ce6120eae10e42393746eb0e02ecae9") or SHA1 in~ ("84a6ccaaab1596139d28e822f40cc99c68d337d4c81d1c6d9692c1d6bb22e4af", "6044974c633b3a319c31bb32110411520c425e89722a64806528553227e7a50a", "0910ecfa049738ef3f2540855341a380df89224ff71da94b4c21689fd66f62e3", "b8b81af76163bdcc5b4f7d8fe6795f164991f8a62678c971db031b9e90a27813", "ef9a1896eeaae929800eade768276e2240ef252d26d0d96c1950a1a5e1aadb34", "e5d8350f1540fe91145dc262c455bca7748ad97dafb2d9facd5adebed9f66d2d", "41957bd0ba2d9c07af2e069f10780fdf6b2102c065bebe0db2136dfe07d67a28", "33b58598eb317553942e27545982d4c25ce6120eae10e42393746eb0e02ecae9") or MD5 in~ ("84a6ccaaab1596139d28e822f40cc99c68d337d4c81d1c6d9692c1d6bb22e4af", "6044974c633b3a319c31bb32110411520c425e89722a64806528553227e7a50a", "0910ecfa049738ef3f2540855341a380df89224ff71da94b4c21689fd66f62e3", "b8b81af76163bdcc5b4f7d8fe6795f164991f8a62678c971db031b9e90a27813", "ef9a1896eeaae929800eade768276e2240ef252d26d0d96c1950a1a5e1aadb34", "e5d8350f1540fe91145dc262c455bca7748ad97dafb2d9facd5adebed9f66d2d", "41957bd0ba2d9c07af2e069f10780fdf6b2102c065bebe0db2136dfe07d67a28", "33b58598eb317553942e27545982d4c25ce6120eae10e42393746eb0e02ecae9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("84a6ccaaab1596139d28e822f40cc99c68d337d4c81d1c6d9692c1d6bb22e4af", "6044974c633b3a319c31bb32110411520c425e89722a64806528553227e7a50a", "0910ecfa049738ef3f2540855341a380df89224ff71da94b4c21689fd66f62e3", "b8b81af76163bdcc5b4f7d8fe6795f164991f8a62678c971db031b9e90a27813", "ef9a1896eeaae929800eade768276e2240ef252d26d0d96c1950a1a5e1aadb34", "e5d8350f1540fe91145dc262c455bca7748ad97dafb2d9facd5adebed9f66d2d", "41957bd0ba2d9c07af2e069f10780fdf6b2102c065bebe0db2136dfe07d67a28", "33b58598eb317553942e27545982d4c25ce6120eae10e42393746eb0e02ecae9") or SHA1 in~ ("84a6ccaaab1596139d28e822f40cc99c68d337d4c81d1c6d9692c1d6bb22e4af", "6044974c633b3a319c31bb32110411520c425e89722a64806528553227e7a50a", "0910ecfa049738ef3f2540855341a380df89224ff71da94b4c21689fd66f62e3", "b8b81af76163bdcc5b4f7d8fe6795f164991f8a62678c971db031b9e90a27813", "ef9a1896eeaae929800eade768276e2240ef252d26d0d96c1950a1a5e1aadb34", "e5d8350f1540fe91145dc262c455bca7748ad97dafb2d9facd5adebed9f66d2d", "41957bd0ba2d9c07af2e069f10780fdf6b2102c065bebe0db2136dfe07d67a28", "33b58598eb317553942e27545982d4c25ce6120eae10e42393746eb0e02ecae9") or MD5 in~ ("84a6ccaaab1596139d28e822f40cc99c68d337d4c81d1c6d9692c1d6bb22e4af", "6044974c633b3a319c31bb32110411520c425e89722a64806528553227e7a50a", "0910ecfa049738ef3f2540855341a380df89224ff71da94b4c21689fd66f62e3", "b8b81af76163bdcc5b4f7d8fe6795f164991f8a62678c971db031b9e90a27813", "ef9a1896eeaae929800eade768276e2240ef252d26d0d96c1950a1a5e1aadb34", "e5d8350f1540fe91145dc262c455bca7748ad97dafb2d9facd5adebed9f66d2d", "41957bd0ba2d9c07af2e069f10780fdf6b2102c065bebe0db2136dfe07d67a28", "33b58598eb317553942e27545982d4c25ce6120eae10e42393746eb0e02ecae9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["84a6ccaaab1596139d28e822f40cc99c68d337d4c81d1c6d9692c1d6bb22e4af", "6044974c633b3a319c31bb32110411520c425e89722a64806528553227e7a50a", "0910ecfa049738ef3f2540855341a380df89224ff71da94b4c21689fd66f62e3", "b8b81af76163bdcc5b4f7d8fe6795f164991f8a62678c971db031b9e90a27813", "ef9a1896eeaae929800eade768276e2240ef252d26d0d96c1950a1a5e1aadb34", "e5d8350f1540fe91145dc262c455bca7748ad97dafb2d9facd5adebed9f66d2d", "41957bd0ba2d9c07af2e069f10780fdf6b2102c065bebe0db2136dfe07d67a28", "33b58598eb317553942e27545982d4c25ce6120eae10e42393746eb0e02ecae9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google Password Manager Attacks Could Let Malware Hijack Passkey-Protected Accounts

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 9 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Malware running as an ordinary user on a Windows machine can sign into a victim's passkey-protected accounts without a fingerprint, a PIN, or anything at all appearing on the victim's screen. Unit 42 detailed three attack paths against Chrome's Google Password Manager cloud authenticator, which it calls Pass-ta-key, Silver Pass-ta-key and Golden Pass-ta-key; the strongest targets the master key

ATT&CKT1190 T1566 T1566.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Command line referencing Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB path
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Google Password Manager Attacks Could Let Malware Hijack Passkey-Protected Accou
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Chrome process reading chrome.exe memory to steal passkey Security Domain Secret (Golden Pass-ta-key) · [LLM] Non-Chrome process tampering with Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB
Non-Chrome process reading chrome.exe memory to steal passkey Security Domain Secret (Golden Pass-ta-key) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a non-browser process opening a read handle into chrome.exe address space to scrape the 32-byte Security Domain Secret (SDS) while it sits in plaintext during passkey re-enrollment. Unit 42's Golden Pass-ta-key path reads the SDS out of Chrome process memory to decrypt all synced passkey private keys, so any non-Chrome, non-AV process reading Chrome memory is high-signal. Rationale: Uses the exact Golden Pass-ta-key behaviour from the Unit 42 report (SDS read from chrome.exe process memory) via Defender's raw OpenProcessApiCall/ReadProcessMemoryApiCall telemetry and Sysmon EID 10, scoping TargetImage=chrome.exe and excluding Chrome's own processes and AV. Datadog/Falcon left blank because neither the provided Sysmon EID subset nor an FDR process-access simpleName cleanly expresses cross-process read handles. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-authenticators-hidden-passkey-architecture/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Defender (MsMpEng.exe) scanning Chrome memory
  • Endpoint DLP / EDR agents inspecting browser processes
  • Task Manager or Process Explorer opened by an admin to inspect Chrome
  • Crash-reporting tools (crashpad_handler) reading Chrome on a hang
  • Browser performance/telemetry agents with legitimate read access
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","taskmgr.exe","procexp64.exe","procexp.exe","MpDefenderCoreService.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Google\Chrome\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 and folder path of the reader; confirm it is not AV/DLP/crashpad and is not signed by Google. Check GrantedAccess mask for PROCESS_VM_READ and whether the process was newly written to disk. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process, and force a Google account passkey/SDS re-enrollment and PIN change for the signed-in user (assume all synced passkeys are compromised). 3) Hunt: pivot on the reader's SHA256 across the fleet, check for prior file access to passkey_enclave_state / Sync Data LevelDB, and review the affected Google account for anomalous passkey assertions or new device enrollments.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("OpenProcessApiCall", "ReadProcessMemoryApiCall")
| where FileName =~ "chrome.exe"                       // target process being read = Chrome
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"      // Chrome's own multi-process reads are legit
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Google\Chrome\"   // exclude crashpad_handler / updater
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","taskmgr.exe","procexp64.exe","procexp.exe","csrss.exe","wininit.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcess = FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 10   // ProcessAccess
| where EventData has "chrome.exe"                                // TargetImage
| where EventData has_any ("0x1010","0x1410","0x1438","0x143a","0x1fffff","0x0010")  // GrantedAccess incl PROCESS_VM_READ
| where EventData !has @"\Google\Chrome\"                        // exclude Chrome/updater as the source
| where EventData !has "MsMpEng.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Chrome Process Reads Chrome Memory (Passkey SDS Theft)
id: 8f3a1d2e-6b74-4c9a-9e21-5c0f7a2b1d44
description: Detects a non-browser process opening a read handle into chrome.exe to scrape the passkey Security Domain Secret (Unit 42 Golden Pass-ta-key)
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.003
logsource:
  category: process_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetImage|endswith: '\chrome.exe'
    GrantedAccess|contains:
      - '0x1010'
      - '0x1410'
      - '0x1438'
      - '0x143a'
      - '0x1fffff'
  filter_chrome:
    SourceImage|contains: '\Google\Chrome\'
  filter_known:
    SourceImage|endswith:
      - '\MsMpEng.exe'
      - '\taskmgr.exe'
      - '\procexp64.exe'
  condition: selection and not (filter_chrome or filter_known)
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chrome.exe) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search parent_process_name!=chrome.exe AND parent_process!="*\\Google\\Chrome\\*" AND parent_process_name!="MsMpEng.exe" AND parent_process_name!="taskmgr.exe" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chrome.exe) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search parent_process_name!=chrome.exe AND parent_process!="*\\Google\\Chrome\\*" AND parent_process_name!="MsMpEng.exe" AND parent_process_name!="taskmgr.exe" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Non-Chrome process tampering with Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a non-Chrome process writing, copying, renaming, or deleting Chrome's passkey device-key store (passkey_enclave_state) or the synced-credential LevelDB. Copy-out feeds offline SDS/passkey recovery; deletion forces the device re-enrollment window that Silver/Golden Pass-ta-key abuse to register an attacker UV key. Rationale: Anchored on the exact artifacts named in the Unit 42 report — passkey_enclave_state (wrapped device key + SDS + PIN) and the Sync Data\LevelDB WebauthnCredentialSpecifics store — with any non-Chrome, non-Google-signed writer/deleter surfaced. Deletion maps to the forced re-enrollment window abused by Silver/Golden; copy-out maps to offline recovery. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1556
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive / enterprise backup agents syncing the Chrome profile folder
  • Chrome profile migration or roaming-profile tooling
  • Antivirus quarantine touching files under User Data
  • Admin manually deleting a corrupt Chrome profile to fix sync
  • Endpoint management agents wiping browser data on offboarding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MpDefenderCoreService.exe","backup.exe","cbsystray.exe") and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "Google LLC"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is not Google-signed, OneDrive, or backup software; note ActionType (Delete vs Create/Modify) and whether a copy of passkey_enclave_state / LevelDB landed outside the profile. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill/quarantine the process, and treat the user's synced passkeys as compromised — trigger passkey re-enrollment and PIN rotation on the Google account. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (chrome.exe memory reads) on the same host, search for exfil of the copied store over the network, and review the Google account for new device enrollments or attacker-registered UV keys.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
      or (FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and FolderPath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "Google LLC"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Google\Chrome\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","backup.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
      or (TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and TargetFilePath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\chrome.exe"
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\Google\Chrome\"
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\OneDrive.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Command line referencing Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB path AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts LOLBins/scripts (cmd, powershell, esentutl, robocopy, xcopy) invoked with Chrome's passkey store path on the command line — the tooling-based variant of Pass-ta-key local reconnaissance that enumerates relying parties, usernames and encrypted passkey material. Rationale: Targets the article's stated local-recon step (reading credential IDs, relying parties and usernames from Sync Data\LevelDB) plus the passkey_enclave_state path from the Unit 42 report, catching the copy/enumeration variant that uses native tooling rather than in-process API reads. Lower confidence/hunting tier because sophisticated malware reads via API and leaves nothing on the command line. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1217 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Support/IT scripts backing up or clearing a Chrome profile
  • Forensic/DFIR triage collection referencing the LevelDB path
  • Browser-data migration utilities
  • Developer debugging Chrome sync with the path in a script
  • Security tooling that inventories browser credential stores
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and not (AccountName has_any ("svc-dfir","admin-backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full command line and parent process — is this an admin/DFIR script, a migration tool, or an unexpected LOLBin (esentutl/robocopy/powershell) run by a standard user? Check the executing account and host role. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host and kill the process; preserve any output/copy of the passkey store for IR and rotate the affected Google account passkeys. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent process and user to UC1/UC2 (chrome memory reads and file tamper), check for archive/exfil of the collected data, and sweep the fleet for the same command-line pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("passkey_enclave_state", @"Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data" or ProcessCommandLine has "passkey_enclave_state"
| where FileName !~ "chrome.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("passkey_enclave_state", @"Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "passkey_enclave_state"
| where TargetProcessName !has @"\chrome.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection:

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*passkey_enclave_state* OR *PASSKEY_ENCLAVE_STATE* OR *Sync?Data\\LevelDB*) NOT @Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\CHROME.EXE)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

SonicWall SMA 1000 /wsproxy SSRF exploitation (CVE-2026-15409, UTA0533/INC) AIExploitation High
Hunts UTA0533/INC-Ransomware exploitation of the SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF flaw CVE-2026-15409 via crafted /wsproxy requests that pivot the appliance to internal SSH/services. Article-specific because it keys on the exact exploit query-string (serviceType=SSH, host=0.0.0.0, bmID=-3389) and the 'SMA Connect Agent' user-agent Volexity observed. Rationale: Uses Volexity's exact CVE-2026-15409 exploit signature (GET /wsproxy?bmID=-3389&serviceType=SSH&host=0.0.0.0) plus the 'SMA Connect Agent' user-agent. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: the SMA 1000 is a Linux appliance whose inbound HTTP is only visible in appliance/CEF web logs, not endpoint EDR or AWS/Datadog standard sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-sma1000-flaws-exploited-as-zero-days-to-push-custom-malware/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/21/sonicwall-sma-zero-days-exploited-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SonicWall SMA Connect Agent client establishing bookmark/proxy sessions to authorized hosts
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing /wsproxy during a scheduled scan window
  • SonicWall support/diagnostics tooling reproducing wsproxy calls
  • Authorized red-team/pentest engagement against the appliance
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication =~ "SMA Connect Agent" and RequestURL !has "host=0.0.0.0" and RequestURL !has "bmID=-3389")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all /wsproxy hits from the SourceIP; confirm whether serviceType/host/port point at internal RFC1918 targets (real exploitation) vs authorized bookmark hosts. Check if SourceIP is an ExpressVPN/Mullvad exit (UTA0533 pattern). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter, force the SMA 1000 to the mid-July 2026 patched firmware, and isolate the appliance from the internal LAN pending review. 3) Hunt: search the same appliance for the ORANGETAIL/Suo5 gating UA (UC2), for deploy_new.py/xzfind (UC3), and for tcpdump LDAP capture (UC4); rotate all VPN credentials and TOTP MFA seeds.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "SonicWall" or DeviceProduct has "SMA"
| where (RequestURL has "/wsproxy" and (RequestURL has "serviceType=SSH" or RequestURL has "host=0.0.0.0" or RequestURL has "bmID=-3389")) or RequestClientApplication =~ "SMA Connect Agent"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA ORANGETAIL/Suo5 web-shell access via hardcoded gating user-agent AIInstallation High
Detects requests to the ORANGETAIL Java web shell and Suo5 proxy planted on SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances, which are gated behind a hardcoded, fabricated user-agent (Mozilla/6.0 ... Chrome/149.0.0.1) and reached through nginx-rewritten error.jsp routes. Article/Volexity-specific: 'Mozilla/6.0' and 'Chrome/149.0.0.1' are non-existent versions unique to this campaign. Rationale: Keys on the campaign-unique gating user-agent (Mozilla/6.0 with Chrome/149.0.0.1 - both fabricated versions) plus the nginx-rewritten error.jsp routes Volexity documented for ORANGETAIL/Suo5. The UA alone is near-zero-FP because those version tokens do not exist in real browsers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-exploit-sonicwall-sma-zero-days-to-gain-root-access/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users hitting /workplace/error.jsp or errorDialog.jsp during normal SMA portal error handling (UA-only rule avoids this)
  • Security scanners deliberately spoofing malformed user-agents against the portal
  • Synthetic uptime/monitoring probes configured with a custom UA string
  • Browser QA testing with an overridden user-agent
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting SourceIP and whether the fabricated UA appears alongside error.jsp/errorDialog.jsp access; a match on the UA is effectively confirmation of web-shell interaction. 2) Contain: isolate the SMA 1000 from the LAN, block the SourceIP, and image the appliance before rebuild - do not just patch, the web shell is JVM-injected. 3) Hunt: inspect /var/lib/unit/conf.json for the 127.0.0.1:8085 proxy route, look for deploy_new.py and the /tmp/agent_wp8.jar & agent_wp9.jar drops (UC3), and review internal auth for lateral movement tunneled via Suo5.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "SonicWall" or DeviceProduct has "SMA"
| where (RequestClientApplication has "Mozilla/6.0" and RequestClientApplication has "Chrome/149.0.0.1")
    or RequestURL has_any ("/__api__/login","/__api__/logout","/workplace/error.jsp","/workplace/dialogs/errorDialog.jsp")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

KNUCKLEBALL loader, JAR payload drops & init.d persistence on SonicWall SMA AIInstallation High
Hunts the KNUCKLEBALL Python loader (deploy_new.py in the python3.11 site-packages dir), its two staged JARs (agent_wp8.jar=Suo5, agent_wp9.jar=ORANGETAIL), the xzfind ROOTRUN privesc binary, and the /etc/init.d/workplace persistence edit on compromised SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances. Entirely article/Volexity-specific file artifacts. Rationale: Uses Volexity's exact malware paths (deploy_new.py in site-packages, /tmp/agent_wp8.jar & agent_wp9.jar, /usr/bin/xzfind ROOTRUN, /tmp/1234.sh) plus the 'running hotfix removal for:../' path-traversal log string. SHA256s (8c470301..., ea9154e3..., 1e1e68bb..., 81a9af38...) match these files. Falcon/Defender empty: the appliance is not an EDR-managed host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://socradar.io/blog/sonicwall-sma-knuckleball-malware/
ATT&CKT1037.004 T1059.006 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SonicWall firmware/hotfix updates writing to site-packages or modifying /etc/init.d/workplace
  • Vendor support scripts staged under /tmp during a diagnostics session
  • Admin-authored maintenance scripts named similarly in /tmp
  • Backup/AV agents reading (not writing) these paths
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash any deploy_new.py / xzfind / *.jar present and compare to the Volexity SHA256s (deploy_new.py=8c470301..., xzfind=81a9af38..., agent_wp9.jar/ORANGETAIL=ea9154e3..., agent_wp8.jar/Suo5=1e1e68bb...). 2) Contain: power-isolate and rebuild the appliance from clean firmware - JVM-injected payloads survive simple file deletion; remove the deploy_new.py line from /etc/init.d/workplace. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC4 (tcpdump LDAP capture), review /var/lib/unit/conf.json for the 8085 proxy route, and rotate credentials/TOTP seeds harvested from the appliance.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("deploy_new.py","/tmp/agent_wp8.jar","/tmp/agent_wp9.jar","/usr/bin/xzfind","/tmp/1234.sh","running hotfix removal for:../")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

tcpdump LDAP credential sniffing on SonicWall SMA appliance AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the UTA0533 credential-harvesting step where tcpdump is run on a compromised SonicWall SMA appliance to capture cleartext LDAP (TCP 389) authentication traffic, driven by the /var/tmp/lib.sh helper. Article/Volexity-specific credential-access behaviour on the appliance itself. Rationale: Uses Volexity's documented credential-harvesting command (tcpdump on TCP 389 for cleartext LDAP) and the /var/tmp/lib.sh storage helper. Medium confidence/FP because admins do legitimately run tcpdump - the LDAP-389 + /var/tmp/lib.sh combination is the discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.securityweek.com/sonicwall-zero-days-exploited-to-deliver-custom-malware-for-weeks-before-patch/
ATT&CKT1040 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Appliance admin running tcpdump for legitimate LDAP/AD connectivity troubleshooting
  • SonicWall vendor support capturing a diagnostic packet trace
  • Monitoring/observability agents performing periodic packet captures
  • Scheduled config-backup scripts unrelated to lib.sh
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/session that launched tcpdump and whether a capture file was written under /var/tmp; correlate the timestamp to any UC1/UC2 exploitation hit. 2) Contain: kill the tcpdump process, isolate the appliance, and treat all LDAP/AD credentials that authenticated through it as compromised. 3) Hunt: rotate the exposed directory-service credentials and TOTP MFA seeds immediately, then hunt for use of those creds via internal auth logs and for Suo5-tunneled lateral movement.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (SyslogMessage has "tcpdump" and (SyslogMessage has " 389" or SyslogMessage has "port 389" or SyslogMessage has "ldap")) or SyslogMessage has "/var/tmp/lib.sh"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

INC Ransomware encryption: .inc mass file writes and INC-README notes AIActions on Objectives High
Detects INC Ransomware's on-host impact stage on internal Windows endpoints reached via the SonicWall SMA foothold: high-volume file writes/renames to the .inc extension plus creation of INC-README.txt / INC-README.html ransom notes. Enriched from SentinelOne/Huntress INC artifacts since the article names the actor but not the note/extension. Rationale: Article names INC Ransomware as the dominant actor; SentinelOne and Huntress confirm INC writes INC-README.txt/.html notes and appends the .inc extension. The 5-minute >100-file threshold OR any ransom-note write is the mass-encryption discriminator and separates it from benign .inc include files. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/anthology/inc-ransom/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/investigating-new-inc-ransom-group-activity • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer machines mass-writing .inc PHP/ASP/CAD include files during a build (excluded by dev-tool filter + threshold)
  • Backup or archival software touching many files with an .inc-suffixed temp name
  • Legacy applications that legitimately use .inc as a data extension
  • Bulk file-server migration jobs generating high write counts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msbuild.exe","devenv.exe","php.exe","cmake.exe","node.exe") or Notes > 0
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged DeviceName confirm the InitiatingProcess writing .inc files is not a known dev/build tool and that INC-README.txt/.html notes exist; check InitiatingProcessSHA256 against INC IOCs. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network immediately, suspend the offending process, and disable the associated account; snapshot for forensics before any reboot. 3) Hunt: trace the intrusion back to the SMA 1000 (UC1-UC4), check for VSS deletion/backup tampering, and sweep all hosts reachable via the compromised VPN for the same .inc/INC-README pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".inc" or FileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")
| summarize FileCount = count(), Notes = countif(FileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5), Folders = dcount(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileCount > 100 or Notes > 0
| sort by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "inc" or TargetFileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")
| summarize FileCount = count(), Notes = countif(TargetFileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")), SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 5) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileCount > 100 or Notes > 0
| sort by FileCount desc

UTA0533/INC SonicWall exploitation source-IP network IOCs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects endpoint or network communication with the four Volexity-confirmed UTA0533 exploitation/web-shell source IPs (108.205.8.173, 147.45.51.19, 150.241.210.53, 81.19.140.217) used against SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances. Surfaces both inbound appliance interaction and any Suo5-tunneled traffic seen by internal hosts. Rationale: Uses only the four non-VPN sample IPs Volexity published (the campaign also used 200+ ExpressVPN/Mullvad exits, which would be too noisy to ship). Dropped helprans.com and four other article-only IPs (202.8.105.201, 217.77.15.99, 42.200.172.14, 89.117.20.1) as single-source per corroboration rules. Medium confidence because IPs can be reassigned. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195626/hacking/volexity-uncovers-zero-day-campaign-targeting-sonicwall-vpn-appliances.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign users behind a recycled datacenter/VPN IP that was previously attacker-controlled
  • Threat-intel or ASM scanning services legitimately probing your perimeter from a listed IP
  • IP reassigned by the hosting provider to a new tenant after the campaign
  • Internal proxy egressing many users' traffic through one of these addresses
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine direction - inbound to the SMA 1000 (exploitation source) vs an internal host reaching out (possible tunneled C2); pull the process (InitiatingProcessFileName) on any internal hit. 2) Contain: block all four IPs at the perimeter and, for any internal host that contacted them, isolate and inspect for web-shell/Suo5 activity. 3) Hunt: correlate the IP timestamps with UC1/UC2 web-log hits, verify appliance patch level, and rotate credentials/TOTP seeds if the appliance interacted with these IPs.
let iocs = dynamic(["108.205.8.173","147.45.51.19","150.241.210.53","81.19.140.217"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (iocs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| sort by Timestamp desc
let iocs = dynamic(["108.205.8.173","147.45.51.19","150.241.210.53","81.19.140.217"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SrcIpAddr in (iocs) or DstIpAddr in (iocs)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("108.205.8.173", "147.45.51.19", "150.241.210.53", "202.8.105.201", "217.77.15.99", "42.200.172.14", "81.19.140.217", "89.117.20.1")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("helprans.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("helprans.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("108.205.8.173", "147.45.51.19", "150.241.210.53", "202.8.105.201", "217.77.15.99", "42.200.172.14", "81.19.140.217", "89.117.20.1")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("helprans.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("helprans.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or SHA1 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or MD5 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or SHA1 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2") or MD5 in~ ("81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Potato privilege-escalation tooling (GodPotato / SweetPotato / BadPotato) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — An analysis of incidents at Brazilian educational institutions
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] RDP re-enable + EDR/Defender disable batch script (LockBit intrusion) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AnyDesk silent/unattended install used for DragonForce access · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] LockBit payload execution via PsExec service (PsExecSvc.exe → 1.exe/LBB.exe) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
RDP re-enable + EDR/Defender disable batch script (LockBit intrusion) AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-access batch script observed in the leaked-LockBit-builder case that enabled RDP by setting fDenyTSConnections to 0 and disabled endpoint defenses before ransomware deployment. Anchors on the exact registry value/data pair the article's script wrote. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim registry write from the article's disable-defenses batch script (HKLM\...\Control\Terminal Server \ fDenyTSConnections = 0) which turns RDP on; pairs it with reg.exe execution to keep fidelity high. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-builder-leaked-online-by-angry-developer/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately enabling RDP on a new server build via a provisioning script
  • GPO/DSC/Intune configuration baseline that manages fDenyTSConnections
  • MSP onboarding automation that turns on RDP for remote management
  • Server 2016 role-setup wizards that toggle Remote Desktop
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","omadmclient.exe","gpscript.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating account and parent process of the reg.exe/registry write; confirm whether the same host also saw EDR/Defender service stops in the surrounding minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the account used to write the value, and re-set fDenyTSConnections to 1 if the change was unauthorized. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account across DeviceLogonEvents for RDP (LogonType 10) and search for PsExecSvc.exe/named ransomware payloads (1.exe, LBB.exe) and Defender-tamper events fleet-wide.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Terminal Server"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "fDenyTSConnections"
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("SystemSettings.exe","ServerManager.exe","mmc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe"
| where CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections" and CommandLine has_any ("/d 0","/d 0x0")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: RDP Enabled via fDenyTSConnections Registry Modification
id: 8f2b1c40-6d3a-4d1e-9a7b-2f0c9e441a11
description: Detects setting fDenyTSConnections to 0 under the Terminal Server control key, matching the RDP-enable step of the leaked-LockBit-builder intrusion at Brazilian educational institutions.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.t1112
  - attack.t1021.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: registry_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetObject|contains: '\Control\Terminal Server'
    Details: 'DWORD (0x00000000)'
  selection_value:
    TargetObject|endswith: '\fDenyTSConnections'
  condition: selection and selection_value
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@Image:(*\\reg.exe OR *\\REG.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*fDenyTSConnections* OR *FDENYTSCONNECTIONS*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/reg\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/fDenyTSConnections/i
| CommandLine=/\/d\s+0(x0)?/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Control\\Terminal Server*" Registry.registry_value_name="fDenyTSConnections" Registry.registry_value_data="0" by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Control\\Terminal Server*" Registry.registry_value_name="fDenyTSConnections" Registry.registry_value_data="0" by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
LockBit payload execution via PsExec service (PsExecSvc.exe → 1.exe/LBB.exe) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the manual lateral deployment of the custom LockBit build from the leaked builder: the sample was configured without psexec_netspread, so operators used PsExec (PsExecSvc.exe) to remotely launch ransomware binaries named 1.EXE and LBB.exe. Targets the impact/deployment step, not generic PsExec admin use. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim payload names (1.EXE, LBB.exe) and the PsExecSvc.exe service the operators relied on for manual spread after building a variant without psexec_netspread; combining parent + payload names keeps the otherwise-generic 1.exe fidelity acceptable. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware
ATT&CKT1486 T1569.002 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin using Sysinternals PsExec for remote software rollout (PsExecSvc.exe as parent)
  • Automation/RMM that names a tool 1.exe in a temp build path
  • Software packaging test binaries transiently named 1.exe
  • Remote patch scripts pushed via PsExec across a fleet
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\SCCM\\","\\ccmcache\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256 and full path of the spawned binary and the source host driving PsExecSvc.exe; check for mass DeviceFileEvents FileRenamed/FileModified bursts on the same device. 2) Contain: network-isolate affected hosts, block the payload hash, and disable the deploying account. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host where PsExecSvc.exe appeared (USN Journal .KEY artifacts corroborate historic spread), look for kill_defender/Defender-uninstall events and wallpaper/registry changes indicative of LockBit encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "PsExecSvc.exe"
    or FileName in~ ("1.exe","LBB.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\PsExecSvc.exe")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\1.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\LBB.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
