Dataverse table enumeration across Power Pages /_api and /_odata entity sets AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single external source touching many distinct Power Pages Web API/OData entity-set names (with a mix of 200 and 401/403 responses) — the reconnaissance step where an actor maps which Dataverse tables are readable under the Anonymous Users web role before extracting them. Distinct pivot from bulk extraction: keys on breadth of tables probed, not request volume. Rationale: Uses the same article-confirmed '/_api/' and '/_odata' routes but pivots on dcount of distinct entity-set names + a 200/401/403 response mix — the behavioral fingerprint of an actor discovering which Dataverse tables the Anonymous Users role exposes. Aggregation/dcount logic means no Sigma (per rules); no Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch because the telemetry is web-tier only. Cross-checked VenariX and Microsoft Learn. Cross-checked against: • https://venarix.com/blog/exfilsquad-targets-misconfigured-microsoft-power-pages-portals • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/configure/web-api-overview • https://appomni.com/ao-labs/microsoft-power-pages-data-exposure-reviewed/
ATT&CKT1595.003 T1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portal application itself calling several entity sets to render multiple list/grid components in one legitimate session
  • Developers or admins testing Web API table permissions during a portal build/change
  • Authorized security scanners or Power Pages configuration-audit tooling you run yourself
  • Bot/crawler traffic touching multiple portal API paths
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Googlebot","bingbot","UptimeRobot","Azure Traffic Manager Endpoint Monitor")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Review EntitySets for the flagged SrcIpAddr — note whether sensitive tables (contact, systemuser, incident, email) returned 200 (exposed) vs 401/403 (locked). Confirm the source is not a sanctioned integration or internal test. 2) CONTAIN: Remove Anonymous Users read permissions from any table that returned 200, disable the legacy OData feed, and enable the tenant-level anonymous-Dataverse-read block; re-test unauthenticated. 3) HUNT: Search other tenant portals for the same SrcIpAddr/UA and pivot to UC-1 to see if enumeration was followed by bulk extraction from the same source.
let lookback = 24h;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url contains "/_api/" or Url contains "/_odata"   // Power Pages Web API / legacy OData entity-set access
| extend Status = coalesce(HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseCode)
| extend EntitySet = tostring(extract(@"/_(?:api|odata)/([A-Za-z0-9_]+)", 1, Url))
| where isnotempty(EntitySet)
| summarize DistinctEntitySets = dcount(EntitySet),
            EntitySets = make_set(EntitySet, 40),
            Allowed = countif(Status == 200),
            Denied = countif(Status in (401, 403, 404)),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SrcIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| where DistinctEntitySets >= 5   // 5+ distinct Dataverse tables probed by one source = enumeration, not normal browsing
| order by DistinctEntitySets desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_paths, values(Web.status) as statuses, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/_api/*" OR Web.url="*/_odata*") by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent, Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_paths >= 5
| eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), lastTime=strftime(lastTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| sort - distinct_paths
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_paths, values(Web.status) as statuses, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/_api/*" OR Web.url="*/_odata*") by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent, Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_paths >= 5
| eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), lastTime=strftime(lastTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| sort - distinct_paths
Inbound phishing leveraging the PNLD / ExfilSquad breach against named officers AIDelivery Low
Hunts inbound mail whose subject or links reference the PNLD breach lures (PNLD, Police National Legal Database, Ask the Police, ExfilSquad) — the exact follow-on risk UK government guidance flagged, where leaked officer names and work emails make targeted phishing more convincing. Filters out the legitimate breach-notification mail the affected orgs are actually receiving. Rationale: Anchors on the article-specific lure themes (PNLD, Police National Legal Database, Ask the Police, ExfilSquad) that leaked names/work-emails make credible, and explicitly excludes the legitimate pnld.co.uk / ico.org.uk / police.uk breach-notification senders. Low confidence by nature (theme-matching); Sentinel left empty because the provided tenant schema has no EmailEvents-equivalent with reliable Subject content, and Falcon/CloudWatch don't carry O365 mailflow. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/pnld-breach-exposes-uk-police-and.html • https://venarix.com/blog/exfilsquad-targets-misconfigured-microsoft-power-pages-portals • https://hackread.com/microsoft-power-pages-misconfigurations-data-leak/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate breach-notification emails from PNLD, ICO or the affected police forces to staff
  • Internal security-awareness / all-staff advisories referencing the PNLD breach
  • News alerts, threat-intel newsletters or vendor advisories mentioning ExfilSquad / PNLD
  • Journalist or partner enquiries about the incident
Suppression filter
and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "pnld.co.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "ico.org.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "police.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "nationalcrimeagency.gov.uk"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Verify the SenderMailFromDomain and authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC in AuthenticationDetails) — legitimate PNLD/ICO notices will pass and come from expected domains; lookalike or failing-auth senders with a link are suspect. Inspect Url/UrlDomain for credential-harvest pages. 2) CONTAIN: Soft-delete/quarantine confirmed malicious messages tenant-wide via Explorer, block the sender domain and URL, and warn the targeted recipients not to click. 3) HUNT: Pivot on UrlClickEvents for the same URL to find who clicked, and search for the same sender/URL across other affected police-force tenants.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| where Subject has_any ("PNLD","Police National Legal Database","Ask the Police","ExfilSquad") or Subject has_all ("data breach","police")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | take 0) on $left.NetworkMessageId == $left.NetworkMessageId
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| where SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "pnld.co.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "ico.org.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "police.uk"   // strip the genuine breach-notice senders
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, PhishConfidenceLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| where Subject has_any ("PNLD","Police National Legal Database","Ask the Police","ExfilSquad") or Subject has_all ("data breach","police")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | take 0) on $left.NetworkMessageId == $left.NetworkMessageId
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| where SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "pnld.co.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "ico.org.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "police.uk"   // strip the genuine breach-notice senders
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, PhishConfidenceLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Email.subject) as subjects, values(All_Email.src_user) as senders, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email where (All_Email.subject="*PNLD*" OR All_Email.subject="*Police National Legal Database*" OR All_Email.subject="*Ask the Police*" OR All_Email.subject="*ExfilSquad*") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Email.subject) as subjects, values(All_Email.src_user) as senders, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email where (All_Email.subject="*PNLD*" OR All_Email.subject="*Police National Legal Database*" OR All_Email.subject="*Ask the Police*" OR All_Email.subject="*ExfilSquad*") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

N-able Says Attackers Take Over N-central Servers After Initial Fix Proves Incomplete

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 13 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

N-able said attackers exploited an authentication bypass in N-central to gain remote administrative access and reach the customer systems managed through those servers. Its first fix was incomplete. CVE-2026-18577 affects N-central builds prior to 2026.3.1.7. N-able shipped build 2026.3.1.7 on August 2 as the first unaffected version. N-central is the remote monitoring and management platform

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] svchost.exe masquerading in user Documents folder (N-able N-central compromise) · [LLM] Cloudflared tunnel installed as a Windows service (N-central persistence) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — N-able Says Attackers Take Over N-central Servers After Initial Fix Proves Incom
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Cloudflare tunnel outbound egress on TCP/7844 from managed endpoints · [LLM] Endpoint connections to N-able published attacker IPs (N-central takeover) · [LLM] DNS resolution of N-central campaign attacker DDNS domains · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] N-able Take Control agent (BASupSrvc) spawning process enumeration on managed endpoints
svchost.exe masquerading in user Documents folder (N-able N-central compromise) AIInstallation High
Hunts for a process or dropped binary named svchost.exe living under a user's Documents directory, an explicit IOC N-able published for the N-central takeover campaign. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever executes from System32/SysWOW64, so a Documents-path copy is high-fidelity masquerading. Rationale: Uses N-able's own published IOC ('look for svchost.exe in users' Documents folders'). Legitimate svchost only launches from System32/SysWOW64, so path anchoring on Documents yields near-zero benign hits. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog
ATT&CKT1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis or reverse-engineering workstation where an analyst saved a copy of svchost.exe into a Documents folder for study
  • Backup/restore tooling that stages system binaries under a user profile during migration
  • Security-training lab machines demonstrating masquerading techniques
  • A user extracting a memory-forensics capture or triage package containing a copy of svchost.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("7z.exe","winrar.exe","explorer.exe") and FolderPath has "Forensic")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of the Documents svchost.exe and compare to the known-good Microsoft svchost hash; check InitiatingProcessCommandLine and whether the file carries a valid Microsoft signature. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the binary, and confirm whether it is a renamed cloudflared (check for 'tunnel run'/'--token' in the command line). 3) Hunt: on the same host and other endpoints in the same N-central managed group, look for a 'Cloudflared' service, outbound port 7844, and connections to the published attacker IPs/domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where FolderPath has "Documents"
| where FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\svchost.exe"
| where NewProcessName has "Documents"
| where NewProcessName !startswith "C:\\Windows"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloudflared tunnel installed as a Windows service (N-central persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects installation of a Windows service named Cloudflared or a service pointing at a cloudflared tunnel binary, the persistence mechanism N-able reported attackers registered on managed endpoints so access survived reboot and N-central revocation. Rationale: Anchored on N-able's stated IOC ('a service named Cloudflared') and the reported TTP of running Cloudflare tunnels as services for reboot persistence. Service-name/path pivot is precise and rarely benign in managed-endpoint fleets. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.cyber.gov.au
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organisation that legitimately uses Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) for sanctioned remote access installs the service by policy
  • IT admin testing cloudflared for internal web-app publishing
  • A managed-service provider that deploys cloudflared as an approved connectivity tool
  • Automated provisioning scripts that register cloudflared on kiosk/remote hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who/what installed the service (InitiatingProcessCommandLine), the binary path/hash, and whether cloudflared is sanctioned in this environment. 2) Contain: stop and delete the service, kill the cloudflared process, and block outbound port 7844; preserve the binary and tunnel token for IR. 3) Hunt: because upgrading N-central does NOT remove this endpoint persistence, sweep every device in the same N-central account for the Cloudflared service, svchost.exe in Documents, and the published attacker IPs/domains.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| where AdditionalFields has "cloudflared" or AdditionalFields has "tunnel run"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceName has "cloudflared" or ServiceFileName has "cloudflared" or ServiceFileName has "tunnel"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloudflare tunnel outbound egress on TCP/7844 from managed endpoints AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections on TCP/7844 (Cloudflare tunnel/argotunnel control channel) or from a cloudflared process, the outbound-only C2 path attackers used so no inbound firewall rule was needed and access persisted after the N-central route was revoked. Rationale: Grounded on N-able's description of Cloudflare tunnels running as services and connecting outbound to Cloudflare's edge. TCP/7844 is cloudflared's control channel; pairing with the cloudflared process/argotunnel host raises fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/connections/connect-networks/
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned use of Cloudflare Tunnel for remote access or internal app publishing generates the same 7844 egress
  • Developers running 'cloudflared tunnel' for local testing
  • Cloudflare WARP client traffic on some deployments
  • MSP-approved cloudflared connectors on remote sites
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether cloudflared is sanctioned; identify the initiating process, service backing, and the tunnel token/hostname. 2) Contain: block TCP/7844 egress at the firewall, stop/delete the Cloudflared service, and isolate affected hosts. 3) Hunt: correlate 7844 egress with a 'Cloudflared' service, svchost.exe in Documents, and the six published attacker IPs across the N-central-managed fleet; because tunnels persist independently of N-central, remediate each endpoint.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemotePort == 7844 or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "cloudflared" or RemoteUrl has "argotunnel.com"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationPort == 7844 or DestinationHostName has "argotunnel.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint connections to N-able published attacker IPs (N-central takeover) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for outbound connections from managed endpoints or N-central servers to the six IP addresses N-able published for this campaign. Four are Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes (per Huntress), so this is a hunting pivot to be correlated with N-central UI/endpoint logs, not a standalone alert. Rationale: Uses the six exact IPs N-able published. Huntress attributed four to Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes, so this is scoped as a hunting pivot to correlate with N-central UI/network/endpoint logs rather than alert-on-first-hit. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate employees using Mullvad or NordVPN whose exit nodes overlap four of the published IPs (per Huntress)
  • Corporate VPN concentrator sharing an ASN with a listed provider
  • Threat-intel or research boxes deliberately touching the IOCs
  • Shared cloud/VPS ranges where the IP has been reassigned since the campaign
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, verify the source host is an N-central server or managed endpoint and check whether the user legitimately runs a VPN (four IPs are Mullvad/NordVPN). 2) Contain: if the host is an N-central asset or shows corroborating IOCs, isolate it and block the IP. 3) Hunt: correlate matches with ui_access_control.log / BASupSrvc logs, the Cloudflared service, and svchost.exe-in-Documents; expand to sessions tied to mspsupport@n-able.com.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181","68.235.46.214")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181","68.235.46.214")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS resolution of N-central campaign attacker DDNS domains AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS queries for the three Synology DDNS domains Huntress published for the N-central intrusion (mousears.synology.me and two direct.quickconnect.to hosts). Exact-FQDN matching makes this a high-fidelity C2/staging indicator. Rationale: Exact-FQDN match on the three attacker domains Huntress published in its August 3 rapid response. Full-domain matching (not a wildcard on synology.me/quickconnect.to) keeps FPs near zero while still catching the campaign infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user who legitimately owns a Synology NAS reachable via one of these exact quickconnect.to hostnames (unlikely given the specific attacker labels)
  • Security researcher resolving the IOC for validation
  • DNS sinkhole/telemetry appliance re-querying the domains
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling touching the FQDNs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host and the process (ContextImageFileName) that triggered the lookup; confirm it is an N-central asset or managed endpoint. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the three FQDNs, isolate the host, and capture any cloudflared/svchost artifacts. 3) Hunt: pivot from the resolving host to the Cloudflared service, TCP/7844 egress, the published attacker IPs, and N-central Take Control logs (ui_access_control.log, BASupSrvc_*.log.gz).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

N-able Take Control agent (BASupSrvc) spawning process enumeration on managed endpoints AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the N-able Take Control/support agent (GetSupportService_N-Central, BASupSrvc) spawning process-enumeration tools, matching Huntress's observation that post-compromise activity was limited to enumerating running processes on reached endpoints. Flags attacker-driven remote reconnaissance through the RMM agent. Rationale: Parent binary grounded in the article's Take Control log path C:\ProgramData\GetSupportService_N-Central\Logs\BASupSrvc_*.log.gz; child behaviour grounded in Huntress's finding that post-compromise activity was limited to enumerating running processes before disconnect. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog
ATT&CKT1057 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate N-able Take Control session where a technician runs tasklist/Get-Process for real troubleshooting (article notes these logs appear during legitimate use)
  • Automated N-central monitoring scripts that poll running processes
  • Software-inventory or patch pre-checks executed through the RMM agent
  • Helpdesk remote support gathering process lists for a ticket
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "scheduled" and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull ui_access_control.log and BASupSrvc_*.log.gz for the session, and check whether it maps to an authorised technician or to an N-able support identity such as mspsupport@n-able.com. 2) Contain: if unattributed, suspend the Take Control session, rotate N-central operator credentials, and isolate the endpoint. 3) Hunt: on the same endpoint look for the Cloudflared service, svchost.exe in Documents, TCP/7844 egress, and the published IPs/domains; enumerate all nine-ish endpoints reached under the affected partner account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BASupSrvc.exe","BASupApp.exe","BASupSrvcUpdater.exe")
| where (FileName in~ ("tasklist.exe","wmic.exe","qprocess.exe")) or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-Process","tasklist","process list","wmic process"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("BASupSrvc.exe","BASupApp.exe","BASupSrvcUpdater.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\tasklist.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wmic.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\qprocess.exe" or (NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" and CommandLine has "Get-Process")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hugging Face Diffusers Flaws Could Let Model Repositories Execute Arbitrary Code

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 11 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Three high-severity security flaws have been disclosed in Hugging Face's Diffusers library that could allow crafted model repositories to stealthily execute arbitrary code on machines that load it, opening the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain to security risk. "These vulnerabilities are bypassing trust_remote_code, the safeguard designed to stop unreviewed code from running in the

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Untrusted custom-pipeline .py (incl. None.py) staged in Hugging Face cache — FaceHugger · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Python/Diffusers process spawning shell or download utility (FaceHugger RCE execution) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hugging Face Diffusers Flaws Could Let Model Repositories Execute Arbitrary Code
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2/exfil from Python after Diffusers model load (non-Hugging-Face egress) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Untrusted custom-pipeline .py (incl. None.py) staged in Hugging Face cache — FaceHugger AIDelivery High
Hunts the FaceHugger (CVE-2026-44827/44513/45804) trust_remote_code bypass, where DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained pulls a crafted repo that drops executable Python (notably a pipeline literally named None.py, or stray *.py under model component subdirs like unet/ and scheduler/) into the local Hugging Face snapshot/dynamic-module cache. A model snapshot should be weights + JSON — a .py file appearing under it, written by a python interpreter, is the pre-execution artifact of the bypass. Rationale: Uses the article's exact bypass artifacts: the crafted custom_pipeline named None.py (CVE-2026-44827) and the maintainer guidance to inspect snapshots for unexpected *.py under unet/, scheduler/, etc. A .py written by python into the HF cache is high-fidelity because legitimate model snapshots ship weights + JSON, not code.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate custom pipelines from trusted, audited repos that intentionally ship pipeline.py (e.g. community diffusion pipelines the team explicitly uses)
  • Diffusers itself caching its own dynamic modules for a first-party trusted pipeline
  • Data scientist manually copying a reviewed pipeline.py into the local snapshot for testing
  • A repo with a benign helper .py placed at the snapshot root that the team has vetted
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("stabilityai","runwayml","CompVis") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("approved-mlops","ci-builder"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written .py (None.py or the component-subdir file) and read it — look for os.system/subprocess/exec/eval, urllib/requests, base64 blobs. Identify the model repo id from the parent folder path and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the file contains execution/network code; kill the python process; quarantine the file and the whole model snapshot dir; block the source repo. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for child shells spawned by python (UC2) and outbound connections from python (UC3) within minutes of the write; check whether Diffusers < 0.38.0 is installed across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".py"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.cache\huggingface\", "/.cache/huggingface/", "diffusers_modules", @"\huggingface\hub\", "/huggingface/hub/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where FileName =~ "None.py" or FolderPath has_any ("unet","scheduler","vae","text_encoder","tokenizer","feature_extractor","safety_checker")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".py"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("huggingface", "diffusers_modules")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","pythonw")
| where TargetFileName =~ "None.py" or TargetFilePath has_any ("unet","scheduler","vae","text_encoder","tokenizer","feature_extractor","safety_checker")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Untrusted Python custom-pipeline file staged in Hugging Face cache (FaceHugger)
id: 8f3c9e21-4a6d-4c7b-9b2e-1d5f6a7c8e90
description: Detects a python interpreter writing a .py file (notably None.py or stray code under model component subdirectories) into the local Hugging Face snapshot/dynamic-module cache, the pre-execution artifact of the Diffusers trust_remote_code bypass CVE-2026-44827/44513/45804.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hugging-face-diffusers-flaws-could-let.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.cache\huggingface\'
      - 'diffusers_modules'
      - '\huggingface\hub\'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.py'
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
  condition: selection_path and selection_ext and selection_proc
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*huggingface* OR @TargetFilename:*Huggingface* OR @TargetFilename:*diffusers_modules*) @TargetFilename:*.py (@Image:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\.cache[\/\\]huggingface|diffusers_modules|huggingface[\/\\]hub)/i
| TargetFileName=/\.py$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/python(3|w)?(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Python/Diffusers process spawning shell or download utility (FaceHugger RCE execution) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the arbitrary-code-execution stage of FaceHugger: once trust_remote_code is bypassed, the crafted custom pipeline runs inside the loading python process and typically spawns a shell or grabs a second stage. Flags a python parent spawning bash/sh/cmd/powershell where the child command line carries download or encoding indicators — the point where a routine DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained turns into an initial-access vector. Rationale: Directly targets the article's core claim — crafted model repos 'stealthily execute arbitrary code on machines that load it'. Python (the Diffusers host) spawning a shell/downloader with second-stage indicators is the observable RCE moment; the encoding/network indicators keep FPs down versus a bare python->shell rule.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ML build/setup scripts where python legitimately shells out to curl/wget to fetch datasets or wheels
  • Jupyter/IPython '!' bang commands that spawn a shell with curl/wget
  • conda/pip post-install hooks invoking bash with base64-encoded config
  • CI pipeline python wrappers that call powershell -enc for legitimate packaging
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter","ipykernel_launcher","conda","pip install","setup.py","pip._internal") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent python command line and the child command line; decode any base64/-enc payload; determine whether python was loading a Diffusers pipeline (check recent HF cache writes on the host, UC1). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill both processes if the decoded command reaches an external IP or drops a binary; preserve the parent python script and any staged .py. 3) Hunt: enumerate outbound connections from the same python PID/host (UC3), check other hosts that pulled the same model repo id, and confirm Diffusers version — upgrade to >=0.38.0.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","/dev/tcp","base64","-enc","Invoke-WebRequest","IEX","ncat","nc ","bash -i","socket.socket","python -c")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl","wget","ncat")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","/dev/tcp","base64","-enc","Invoke-WebRequest","IEX","ncat","nc ","bash -i","socket.socket","python -c")

Outbound C2/exfil from Python after Diffusers model load (non-Hugging-Face egress) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts post-exploitation network activity from the python process that loaded a malicious Diffusers pipeline (FaceHugger). Surfaces DNS/HTTP egress from python to destinations that are NOT Hugging Face / PyPI / model-CDN infrastructure — beaconing or second-stage retrieval driven by attacker code that ran during from_pretrained. Pairs with UC1 (file staging) and UC2 (subprocess) as the C2 leg of the chain. Rationale: The article states a bypassed model load 'can easily become a vector for arbitrary code execution' running in the user's process; python egress to anything other than the known model/package CDNs is the natural C2/exfil observable. Excluding HF/PyPI/pytorch CDNs isolates the anomalous destinations.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python apps legitimately calling third-party APIs (OpenAI, internal REST services, telemetry endpoints)
  • MLflow / Weights & Biases / HuggingFace-datasets pulling from non-CDN mirrors
  • pip resolving a wheel from a private/internal index not in the allowlist
  • Data pipelines fetching training data from S3/GCS buckets
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("openai.com","wandb.ai","mlflow","s3.amazonaws.com","storage.googleapis.com") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the destination is newly-registered/rare-in-org and whether the same host shows a recent HF cache .py write (UC1) or python->shell spawn (UC2) minutes prior. 2) Contain: block the destination domain/IP at egress, isolate the host if correlated with UC1/UC2, and snapshot the python process memory/args. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for other python hosts contacting the same destination and for the originating model repo id; confirm and patch Diffusers to >=0.38.0.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","hf.co","pythonhosted.org","pypi.org","cloudfront.net","githubusercontent.com","pytorch.org","anaconda.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","hf.co","pythonhosted.org","pypi.org","cloudfront.net","githubusercontent.com","pytorch.org","anaconda.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-18577", "CVE-2026-18556")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-18577", "CVE-2026-18556")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
