Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hunts endpoint or perimeter connections to the hardcoded attacker server 84.32.102.230 on TCP/7744, the exfil endpoint the poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js beacons to on page load (sending victim hostname + path). This IP:port is the single highest-fidelity IOC of the campaign — it exists only in the malicious payload. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the exact exfil IP:port confirmed across the article and second sources (BleepingComputer, Beaumont/DoublePulsar). 1) Triage: identify the source host/user and confirm the initiating process is a browser (msedge/chrome/firefox); pull the RemoteUrl/referrer the browser was on to find which affected website served the poisoned script. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at egress/firewall, and instruct the user to clear browser cache (the malicious trackpoint-async.js may persist cached) and verify any crypto wallet addresses recently copied/pasted. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts that both loaded s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js and beaconed to this IP; alert any user who transacted crypto on July 26-27 2026.

Confirmed Adform supply-chain victim: poisoned script load + beacon to attacker IP AIDelivery High
Correlates hosts that loaded the compromised third-party resource s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js with an outbound beacon to 84.32.102.230 on the same host. The script load alone is benign (Adform is loaded by thousands of legitimate sites); the join with the exfil beacon promotes it to a confirmed supply-chain compromise. Rationale: Combines the two confirmed IOCs (poisoned file path s2.adform.net/.../trackpoint-async.js and exfil IP 84.32.102.230:7744) on a single host. The join eliminates the massive benign-load noise of Adform being a legitimate ad tag, yielding a high-fidelity supply-chain-victim signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared egress/NAT IP causes an unrelated user's script load to correlate with another user's beacon (validate on managed-host DeviceId join in Defender rather than SrcIpAddr)
  • Proxy that rewrites/caches the Adform URL so the recorded host differs from the beaconing host
  • IOC IP reallocated post-takedown to a benign service
  • Falcon variant relies on DNS to s2.adform.net which is a shared CDN host — treat DNS as a weak loader proxy, the beacon is the anchor
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each correlated host confirm the beacon process is a browser and identify the affected first-party website that embedded the tag. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at egress, force browser cache clear on the host, and reset/verify any crypto wallet addresses the user handled. 3) Hunt: enumerate every user who initiated crypto transactions during the exposure window and review outbound transfers for address substitution; notify affected clients per IR policy.

    | where RemoteUrl has "trackpoint-async.js" and RemoteUrl has "adform"
    | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName;

| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230" and RemotePort == 7744
| join kind=inner ScriptLoaders on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let ScriptLoaders = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where Url has "trackpoint-async.js" and HttpHostName has "adform"
    | distinct SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr == "84.32.102.230" and DstPortNumber == 7744
| join kind=inner ScriptLoaders on SrcIpAddr
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| join({#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="84.32.102.230" RemotePort=7744}, field=aid, include=[RemoteAddressIP4])

Exposure scoping: hosts that loaded poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js (Jul 26-28 2026) AIDelivery Medium
IR-scoping hunt that surfaces every managed host which fetched s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js during the compromise window (oldest malicious sample July 26, removed July 27 2026). Used to build the affected-user list for cache-clear guidance and crypto-transaction review, not as a standalone malicious-behaviour alert. Rationale: Anchored on the exact compromised resource path (s2.adform.net/.../trackpoint-async.js) and the confirmed malicious window (sample July 26, removed July 27 2026). Deliberately scoped by date because the file was benign before/after — this is an exposure list, not a malicious-behaviour detection, hence hunting tier and high expected FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that loaded the clean, restored trackpoint-async.js after Adform's July 27 fix (mitigated by the date window)
  • Legitimate marketing/ad-ops staff and QA whose job involves the Adform platform
  • Cached copies replayed after the window, skewing timestamps
  • FDR/Falcon variant keys on DNS to shared host s2.adform.net which serves many benign scripts — treat as broad exposure, not confirmation
Suppression filter
| where FirstSeen between (datetime(2026-07-26) .. datetime(2026-07-28))
Response runbook
1) Triage: treat the output as the exposed-population list; prioritise hosts/users known to handle cryptocurrency. 2) Contain: push guidance to clear browser cache (the poisoned file may remain cached) and to re-verify any wallet address before sending funds. 3) Hunt: cross-reference this list against UC 'Confirmed Adform supply-chain victim' (beacon to 84.32.102.230) to separate merely-exposed from confirmed-compromised, and review crypto transactions initiated during the window for address substitution.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

            - 'invoke-expression'

Hijacked Hotel Wi-Fi Pushes Fake Updates to Deliver Surveillance Malware

The Hacker News
2026-08-01 15 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A fake browser update served over hijacked hotel Wi-Fi has been used to deliver CornFlake, a remote access trojan (RAT) that can capture webcam images, microphone audio, and keystrokes, Microsoft said in its latest report. Researchers track the operation as CaptiveCrunch and attribute it to Storm-2945. It assesses Storm-2945 to be an operational sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard, also known as

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix fake-update command referencing CaptiveCrunch infrastructure · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Microsoft device code authentication flow phishing sign-in · [LLM] CaptiveCrunch C2 / phishing infrastructure network callback · Network connections to article IPs / domains

CornFlake RAT self-copy to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the CornFlake Go implant staging itself as %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe — a masquerade of the legitimate System32 svchost.exe that never legitimately lives in Roaming AppData. This is the on-disk footprint of the CaptiveCrunch implant before service registration. Rationale: Anchors on the exact implant path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe named in Microsoft's report; the '32'-suffixed svchost in Roaming AppData is not a real Windows binary, giving near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche third-party 'svchost32' utility legitimately installed under Roaming (extremely rare)
  • Security researcher / malware analyst detonating a CornFlake sample in a monitored VM
  • Backup or EDR sync agent that copies quarantined samples into a Roaming staging folder
  • Custom LOB app that unfortunately named its binary svchost32.exe (validate publisher/signer)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msmpeng.exe","sense.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Windows Defender")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SHA256 of the created file and the InitiatingProcess; check signer status and whether the parent is a browser/terminal from a captive-portal 'update'. 2) Contain: isolate the host in Defender, kill the svchost32 process tree, and quarantine %APPDATA%\svchost32\. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'CornFlake service Cloud Sync Service' and UC 'ChocoShell Token Broker theft' on the same DeviceId; check outbound to the CaptiveCrunch C2 IOCs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake service registration 'svchost32' / 'Cloud Sync Service' AIInstallation High
Detects registration of the CornFlake persistence service — Windows service name svchost32 with display name 'Cloud Sync Service' and description 'Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider'. This is the service-based persistence layer of the CaptiveCrunch implant, restored by a watchdog if removed. Rationale: Uses the literal service name (svchost32), display name ('Cloud Sync Service'), and ImagePath (svchost32.exe) from Microsoft's write-up — all three are unique campaign strings, so any one match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://www.secnews.gr/en/725008/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-xenodocheia-wifi/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate cloud-sync product coincidentally using display name 'Cloud Sync Service' (verify ImagePath is NOT svchost32.exe in Roaming)
  • EDR/backup agent re-registering a sync service after update
  • Golden-image build process installing sync services (validate against approved software list)
  • Analyst detonation of the sample in a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where not (ServiceFileName has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and ServiceFileName !has "svchost32.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm ServiceFileName resolves to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe (not a signed vendor path); note SubjectUserName that created it. 2) Contain: stop and delete the svchost32 service (sc delete), isolate host — note the watchdog will attempt restore, so remove the file drop, Run key, and scheduled task together. 3) Hunt: enumerate scheduled tasks and HKCU\...\Run entries pointing to svchost32.exe; check other travelers who used the same hotel network for the same service.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\svchost32"
    or (RegistryValueName =~ "DisplayName" and RegistryValueData has "Cloud Sync Service")
    or (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath" and RegistryValueData has "svchost32.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName has "svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChocoShell token theft from TokenBroker .tbres cache AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the ChocoShell in-memory PowerShell stealer reading Microsoft 365 / Entra ID access, refresh and WAM tokens from .tbres files in the Token Broker cache. Any script interpreter (or the svchost32 implant) touching %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\*.tbres is anomalous — legitimate access is by the WAM/TokenBroker host only. Rationale: Anchors on the exact artifact ChocoShell steals — .tbres files in \Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\ — scoped to script interpreters and the svchost32 implant; the public TBRESDecryptor tool confirms this is the real WAM/M365 token store, and normal readers are only the TokenBroker host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://github.com/shackcrack007/TBRESDecryptor
ATT&CKT1528 T1539 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A red-team/purple-team exercise running TBRESDecryptor or ROADtools
  • IT PowerShell script auditing token cache health (rare, validate signer/repo)
  • Endpoint DLP agent indexing AppData (should be its own signed process, not powershell.exe)
  • Developer debugging WAM SSO with a PowerShell helper
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "backgroundTaskHost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full PowerShell command line / script block (correlate with AMSI ScriptControlScanInfo) and the acting user's UPN. 2) Contain: from Entra ID, revoke that user's refresh tokens (revokeSignInSessions) and force password + MFA re-registration; the .tbres theft yields replayable tokens without a browser. 3) Hunt: review SigninLogs/AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for token replay from new IPs/ASNs for that user; pivot to UC 'Device code authentication flow' and the C2 IOC UC.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\"
| where FileName endswith ".tbres"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","svchost32.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".tbres"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","svchost32.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft device code authentication flow phishing sign-in AICommand & Control Medium
Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins that used the OAuth device code flow — the vector CaptiveCrunch landing pages have abused since 16 July to obtain MFA-satisfied, attacker-controlled sessions. Device code flow is rare in most tenants and is Microsoft's recommended Conditional-Access block, so any success is worth review. Rationale: Article states CaptiveCrunch landing pages redirect guests into Microsoft's device code flow since 16 July; device code sign-ins are the article-specific pivot and Microsoft explicitly recommends blocking them via Conditional Access, so the flow's use is inherently high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code onboarding of IoT/CLI tools (Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code', PowerShell Connect-AzAccount)
  • Conference-room / kiosk device provisioning
  • Developers authenticating headless apps or WSL sessions
  • Smart-TV or streaming-device Microsoft account linking
Suppression filter
| where not (AppDisplayName has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and ConditionalAccessStatus == "success")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the IPAddress/Location and UserAgent of the device-code sign-in against the user's normal pattern and whether they were traveling; correlate the sign-in IP with the CaptiveCrunch C2 ranges. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/refresh tokens for the account and, org-wide, deploy a Conditional Access policy blocking device code flow where not required. 3) Hunt: review subsequent app consents, mailbox rules, and token replay from the same session; check other users sharing the venue/IP.

| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, DeviceName, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails) has "Device Code"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch C2 / phishing infrastructure network callback AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host resolving or connecting to the confirmed CaptiveCrunch Microsoft-impersonating domains (m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com, ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, deltaode.com) or the four campaign C2 IPs. Covers both the fake-update/token-phishing landing pages and CornFlake implant callbacks. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the five Microsoft-impersonating domains ReliaQuest and Microsoft both documented plus the four extracted C2 IPs; exact-value matches on known-bad infrastructure are inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox appliance in the org detonating the IOCs
  • Security researcher browsing the phishing domains for analysis from a sanctioned host
  • A parked/sinkholed domain reused by a benign service after takedown (validate IP still hostile)
  • DNS logging test traffic from a SOC validation run
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALWARE-ANALYSIS","TI-DETONATE"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — a browser suggests landing-page interaction; svchost32.exe/powershell suggests active implant C2. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all five domains and four IPs at proxy/firewall/DNS, and add them to the TI platform. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for any historical resolution of these IOCs and pivot to the CornFlake implant-drop and Token Broker theft UCs on matching hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteUrl has_any ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com")
    or RemoteIP in ("31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
    or DstHostname in~ ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClickFix fake-update command referencing CaptiveCrunch infrastructure AIDelivery High
Detects the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix delivery step: a victim pastes an attacker-supplied command into a terminal/Run dialog and a script interpreter (PowerShell, cmd, mshta, curl, certutil, bitsadmin) executes with a command line that references the campaign's phishing/C2 domains or IPs. Captures the actual download cradle that pulls the fake browser/OS update. Rationale: Combines the ClickFix TTP (interpreter running a pasted command) with the campaign's specific infrastructure strings in the command line, surfacing the actual fake-update download cradle rather than a generic interpreter launch. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/analyst running a validation command that includes an IOC domain for testing
  • Threat-hunter pasting an IOC into a terminal while investigating
  • Sanctioned network diagnostics that curl a lookalike domain during takedown validation
  • Automated IOC sweep script that references the domains/IPs as arguments
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC-sweep","threat-hunt","validate-detection"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full ProcessCommandLine to see what was downloaded/executed and identify the parent (explorer.exe = Run-dialog paste is classic ClickFix); note the user and host location. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the interpreter and any spawned installer, block the referenced IOCs. 3) Hunt: check for the CornFlake drop (%APPDATA%\svchost32\), the svchost32 service, scheduled tasks/Run keys, and Token Broker .tbres access on the same host; brief the user on captive-portal update lures.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS SSPP payload: $pullAll/__proto__ PATCH to piece-type API (CVE-2026-53609) AIExploitation High
Hunts the actual exploit request for CVE-2026-53609: a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* whose body carries prototype-pollution keys ($pullAll, __proto__, publicApiProjection, constructor). This is the single most article-specific signal — the poisoning request that mutates Object.prototype.publicApiProjection. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC payload keys from the advisory ($pullAll, __proto__.publicApiProjection) scoped to the /api/v1/@apostrophecms/ PATCH path. Body-token match depends on WAF/proxy body logging — noted in required_telemetry. Fixed version 4.31.0 confirmed via GitLab Advisory DB and TheHackerWire. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/apostrophecms-critical-prototype-pollution-leads-to-auth-bypass/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-53609
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, Nuclei prototype-pollution templates) probing the CMS in an authorized pentest
  • Internal red-team validating CVE-2026-53609 patch status
  • Legitimate editor PATCH that coincidentally contains the literal string 'constructor' in free-text content
  • WAF telemetry replaying blocked-request samples into the SIEM for tuning
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nuclei","nikto","sqlmap","Burp") and SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<authorized_scanner_ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request from WAF/proxy for the flagged SourceIP; confirm the body key is literally __proto__.publicApiProjection (or constructor/prototype) under a $pullAll operator, and note the HTTP response code (200 = poisoning likely succeeded). 2) CONTAIN: If the payload reached the app (not blocked), RESTART the affected Node.js process immediately — pollution persists process-wide until restart — and block the SourceIP at the WAF; verify ApostropheCMS is on <=4.30.0 and schedule upgrade to 4.31.0. 3) HUNT: Search for subsequent unauthenticated 200 responses on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global from any IP after the poisoning timestamp (see companion auth-bypass UC).
let lookback = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("WAF","ModSecurity","Application Gateway","Front Door") or isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection","constructor")

| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS auth-bypass symptom: protected piece-type endpoint 401/403 → 200 transition AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the impact of CVE-2026-53609: a source IP that previously received 401/403 on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user or /global begins receiving 200 responses, without any preceding successful login. This is the process-wide publicApiCheck() bypass observed on the wire. Rationale: Targets the advisory's confirmed observable: /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global flipping from notfound(401/403) to a valid 200 paginated response for unauthenticated callers. Login-IP exclusion asserts the 'unauthenticated' precondition the article emphasises. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1548 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An editor whose session cookie isn't reflected in access logs, appearing 'unauthenticated' while legitimately getting 200
  • publicApiProjection intentionally configured on a piece-type, so unauthenticated 200s are by-design for that endpoint
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor hitting the endpoint from an IP that also fails auth elsewhere
  • CDN edge caching a 200 response and serving it to varied client IPs
Suppression filter
| where uri_path in ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each flagged CIp, confirm the endpoint is one that requires auth by design (user/global) and that no successful /login/login exists for that IP; inspect whether publicApiProjection is legitimately set on the module. 2) CONTAIN: If bypass confirmed, restart the Node.js process to clear Object.prototype pollution and block the offending source IPs; upgrade to 4.31.0. 3) HUNT: Correlate the FirstSuccess timestamp backward ~minutes to find the originating PATCH with $pullAll/__proto__ (companion UC) and identify the editor account whose token performed the poisoning.
let lookback = 3d;
let loggedInIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login" and ScStatus == 200
    | distinct CIp;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where CsMethod =~ "GET"
| where CsUriStem in~ ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
| where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)   // never authenticated -> should never get 200
| summarize AuthFailures = countif(ScStatus in (401,403)),
            Successes = countif(ScStatus == 200),
            LastAuthFail = maxif(TimeGenerated, ScStatus in (401,403)),
            FirstSuccess = minif(TimeGenerated, ScStatus == 200)
            by CIp, CsUriStem
| where Successes > 0 and FirstSuccess > coalesce(LastAuthFail, datetime(1970-01-01))
| project CIp, CsUriStem, AuthFailures, Successes, LastAuthFail, FirstSuccess
| order by Successes desc

ApostropheCMS exploit chain: unauth PATCH to /@apostrophecms/global → 200 GET on /user within 30s AIExploitation High
Correlates the two-step CVE-2026-53609 exploit: a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* from an IP that never authenticated, immediately followed (≤30s) by a successful 200 GET on a normally-protected piece-type endpoint from the same IP. Sequencing raises confidence over either event alone. Rationale: Encodes the PoC step sequence from the advisory (Step 3 PATCH poisoning -> Step 4 unauthenticated 200 on /user) as a same-source temporal join with a 30s window and a never-authenticated precondition, yielding a high-fidelity, low-FP correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated vulnerability scanner running the exact PoC sequence during an authorized assessment
  • Editor whose auth cookie is stripped from access logs, so a legitimate PATCH+GET pair looks unauthenticated
  • Reverse proxy that rewrites method/path causing spurious PATCH-then-GET pairing
  • publicApiProjection legitimately enabled, making the trailing GET a by-design 200
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve both correlated requests for the CIp; confirm the PATCH body carried $pullAll/__proto__ and the GET returned a real result set rather than notfound. 2) CONTAIN: Restart the Node.js process to purge the polluted prototype, block the source IP, and rotate/disable any editor account whose token appears on the PATCH. 3) HUNT: Expand the window to enumerate every unauthenticated 200 to all piece-type endpoints after PatchTime; check for data exfiltration volume and pivot on the editor account for prior suspicious PATCH activity.
let win = 30s;
let lookback = 2d;
let loggedInIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login" and ScStatus == 200
    | distinct CIp;
let patches = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsMethod =~ "PATCH" and CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
    | where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)
    | project PatchTime = TimeGenerated, CIp, PatchUri = CsUriStem;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where CsMethod =~ "GET" and ScStatus == 200
| where CsUriStem in~ ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
| where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)
| join kind=inner patches on CIp
| where TimeGenerated between (PatchTime .. PatchTime + win)
| project PatchTime, GetTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, PatchTime), CIp, PatchUri, GetUri = CsUriStem
| order by PatchTime desc

Exposed ApostropheCMS instances (CVE-2026-53609) asset-exposure hunt AIReconnaissance Low
Inventories which internet-facing hosts/sites serve ApostropheCMS piece-type REST endpoints (/@apostrophecms/), so the SOC can scope CVE-2026-53609 exposure and prioritise upgrade to 4.31.0. A discovery/hunting sweep, not an alert. Rationale: The advisory names the product family (ApostropheCMS) and vulnerable range (<=4.30.0, fixed 4.31.0). Enumerating hosts serving /@apostrophecms/ endpoints is the concrete, log-derivable way to scope exposure without inventing version banners. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-53609
ATT&CKT1592
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Every legitimate ApostropheCMS site in the estate appears — this is inventory, not malice
  • Static asset requests under /@apostrophecms/ media paths inflating counts
  • Internal staging/dev instances mixed with production hosts
  • Third-party or vendor-hosted Apostrophe sites appearing in shared proxy logs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each host/site returned, confirm it is genuinely ApostropheCMS and determine the running version (check package.json / release notes / vendor). 2) CONTAIN: For any instance <=4.30.0, prioritise upgrade to 4.31.0 and apply the __proto__/constructor/prototype path-segment rejection; restrict editor account provisioning. 3) HUNT: On confirmed-vulnerable hosts, run the payload-detection and auth-bypass UCs retroactively over 30d to check for prior exploitation.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CsUriStem has "/@apostrophecms/"
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SamplePaths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20)
            by CsHost
| order by Requests desc

    where (Processes.process_name IN ("node.js"))
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name,
       Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| append [
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified")
      AND (Filesystem.file_name IN ("node.js"))
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]
Critical

CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-31 17 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, has been observed compromising the sign-in portals of hospitality-related organizations such as hotels since May 2026 in order to deliver malware to travelers and steal credentials in an operation we call CaptiveCrunch. The post CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix execution reaching CaptiveCrunch infrastructure or dropping svchost32 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware deliver
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake RAT persistence via svchost32.exe masquerade in %APPDATA% · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint connections to Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch AiTM doppelganger infrastructure · [LLM] CornFlake C2 egress from masqueraded svchost32.exe in AppData · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Entra ID sign-in or session from Storm-2945 AiTM device-code phishing infrastructure · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CornFlake RAT persistence via svchost32.exe masquerade in %APPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts Storm-2945's CornFlake implant, which copies itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and registers as a Windows service 'svchost32' (display name 'Cloud Sync Service') to masquerade as the legitimate System32 svchost.exe. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever runs from %SystemRoot%\System32, so any svchost32.exe under a user profile path is malicious by construction. Rationale: Anchored on the exact drop path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and service name 'svchost32'/'Cloud Sync Service' from the article; corroborated by ReliaQuest and The Hacker News. A binary named svchost32.exe outside System32 has no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche third-party app that legitimately ships a file literally named svchost32.exe in AppData (extremely rare; none known)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the CornFlake sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • EDR sample-detonation or red-team emulation of this exact campaign
  • Backup/restore of an already-infected profile re-writing the path
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the SHA256 of svchost32.exe and confirm the parent process and the '\svchost32\svchost32.exe' path is under a user profile (never System32). Check for a service named svchost32 with display 'Cloud Sync Service'. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop and delete the svchost32 service, remove the Run key and scheduled task pointing at the binary, and force-revoke the user's Entra sessions/tokens (traveler likely token-compromised). 3) HUNT: Sweep for the same path/service org-wide, and pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from svchost32.exe and to the doppelganger M365 domains/IOC IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" or FileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=NewProcessName, Detail=CommandLine, Actor=SubjectUserName),
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4697 | where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=ServiceName, Detail=ServiceFileName, Actor=SubjectUserName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint connections to Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch AiTM doppelganger infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections and DNS lookups to the Storm-2945 doppelganger domains that mimic Microsoft 365 services (ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com) and the campaign's actor-controlled IP infrastructure used for adversary-in-the-middle device-code phishing and M365 token theft. These are hard IOCs — any hit indicates a traveler routed through the CaptiveCrunch AiTM proxy. Rationale: Uses the article's exact doppelganger domain list and pre-extracted actor IP set (Block 2), cross-checked against ReliaQuest's write-up of the same infrastructure. These are unique lookalike domains with zero legitimate business use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security tool / TI feed pre-fetching or sinkholing these IOC domains for analysis
  • Analyst manually browsing to the domain during investigation from a corporate host
  • Passive DNS / URL-scanning services running from the monitored range
  • IP reuse after takedown where the IP is reassigned to a benign host (verify domain hit alongside IP)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify which user/device connected and whether the connection carried an M365 auth flow (browser process, Referer to login.microsoftonline.com). Confirm the device was on untrusted Wi-Fi (hotel/conference). 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's Entra refresh tokens and sign-in sessions immediately, require re-registration of MFA, and block the domains/IPs at proxy and firewall. 3) HUNT: Check Entra sign-in logs for the same user authenticating from the actor IPs and for any new device registration; sweep the endpoint for CornFlake (svchost32.exe) delivered on the same session.

Entra ID sign-in or session from Storm-2945 AiTM device-code phishing infrastructure AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects successful Entra ID authentications originating from Storm-2945's actor-controlled IP infrastructure, the tail end of the CaptiveCrunch device-code AiTM flow where a phished traveler's device code authenticates the attacker's session. Anchors on the campaign's confirmed IP set as the sign-in source. Rationale: Anchors on the article's actor IP set as the authentication source — a successful M365 sign-in from CaptiveCrunch infrastructure is a direct token-theft indicator; Volexity independently documents the same device-code AiTM technique for this actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/02/13/multiple-russian-threat-actors-targeting-microsoft-device-code-authentication/ • https://phishingtackle.com/blog/russian-hackers-use-microsoft-device-code-phishing-in-targeted-attacks
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528 T1098.005
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned by its hosting provider to a benign VPN/proxy a legitimate user transits
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance replaying sign-in test traffic
  • Corporate egress NAT coincidentally sharing a subnet with a taken-down IOC (verify exact /32)
  • Analyst reproducing the auth flow from an actor IP in a lab tenant
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the sign-in succeeded (ErrorCode/ResultType 0) and identify the app (Graph, OWA) and whether a new device was registered in the same window. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke all refresh tokens for the account, disable the account or force password reset + MFA re-enrollment, and remove any attacker-registered device from Entra. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the account to Graph/EWS mail-access and any OAuth app consent grants; check the user's endpoint for CornFlake and correlate to the doppelganger-domain connections from UC2.

ClickFix execution reaching CaptiveCrunch infrastructure or dropping svchost32 AIDelivery High
Detects the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix chain where a user is socially engineered (fake browser/OS update) into running a script interpreter whose command line reaches Storm-2945's doppelganger domains/IOC IPs or references the CornFlake drop path svchost32. Anchors the generic ClickFix pattern to this campaign's concrete IOCs to avoid template noise. Rationale: Pairs the ClickFix execution primitive (interpreter launch) with the campaign's hard IOCs (doppelganger domains, actor IPs, svchost32 drop path) so it fires only on this campaign, not on generic scripting — combination is high-fidelity per the article's ClickFix delivery description. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin script that legitimately references a host named 'svchost32' (rare; verify path context)
  • Security testing/red-team emulating the ClickFix chain in a lab
  • Threat-hunting query copy-pasted into a console leaving IOC strings in a shell history/command line
  • Sinkhole or research tooling curling the IOC domains for analysis
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full command line — confirm which IOC it hit (domain download vs svchost32 reference) and the parent process (explorer.exe/browser indicates ClickFix paste). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the interpreter and any child svchost32.exe, and revoke the user's Entra tokens (traveler credential exposure). 3) HUNT: Pivot to DeviceFileEvents for the svchost32 drop and DeviceNetworkEvents for follow-on C2 to the IOC IPs; sweep other travelers for the same ClickFix command shape.
