CornFlake C2 egress from masqueraded svchost32.exe in AppData AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound network connections initiated by the CornFlake implant running as svchost32.exe from a user AppData path. The legitimate svchost.exe lives only in System32 and its network activity is service-mediated, so public-internet egress from a profile-resident svchost32.exe is CornFlake C2 / data exfiltration beaconing. Rationale: Anchors on the CornFlake implant image/path (svchost32.exe under AppData, from the article) making outbound public connections — behaviorally impossible for the real System32 svchost.exe, so any hit is CornFlake beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox detonation of the CornFlake sample generating C2 traffic on a monitored host
  • Red-team emulation using a binary named svchost32.exe
  • A misconfigured third-party tool coincidentally named svchost32.exe (none known)
  • EDR telemetry replay/testing environments
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm InitiatingProcessFolderPath is a user AppData path and capture the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl destinations (correlate to the campaign IOC IPs). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, terminate svchost32.exe, remove its service/Run key/scheduled task persistence, and block the C2 destinations. 3) HUNT: Retrieve collected-data artifacts (keylogger/screenshot/audio files), revoke the traveler's Entra tokens, and sweep the fleet for the same process-to-public-IP pattern and the svchost32 drop path.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

NocoBase CVE-2026-52887 SQLi in /api/myInAppChannels:list filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt] AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact injection vector: a request to the myInAppChannels:list resource whose filter carries the latestMsgReceiveTimestamp[$lt] parameter loaded with PostgreSQL SQLi primitives (PG_SLEEP, stacked COPY ... TO PROGRAM, CASE WHEN oracles). The legit value of $lt is an epoch integer, so any SQL keyword in this parameter is high-fidelity exploitation of CVE-2026-52887. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable resource string 'myInAppChannels', the injectable parameter 'latestMsgReceiveTimestamp', and the article's live-verified payload tokens PG_SLEEP / COPY ... TO PROGRAM / CASE WHEN. A legit $lt is an integer epoch, so any SQL keyword in this param is exploitation, not noise. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/pull/9001
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest / sqlmap scan against the NocoBase instance (article notes sqlmap 1.10.3 reproduces this)
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Nuclei) firing the CVE-2026-52887 template
  • Security researcher validating the patch on a staging host
  • WAF in monitor-only mode logging blocked-but-recorded attempts
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0")  // add authorized scanner / pentest source IPs here
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request URL and source IP; confirm the $lt value contains SQL rather than a bare integer, and check the response status/latency (a ~5s delay = successful PG_SLEEP oracle). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/proxy, and if the request succeeded, treat the NocoBase DB container as compromised — rotate the super-admin credential and disable allowSignUp. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP for prior /api/auth:signUp and /api/auth:signIn calls, and check the Postgres host for postgres-spawned shell processes (UC3).

| where Url has "myInAppChannels"
| where Url has "latestMsgReceiveTimestamp"
| where Url has_any ("pg_sleep","PG_SLEEP","TO PROGRAM","TO%20PROGRAM","COPY","CASE WHEN","CASE%20WHEN","UNION","pg_read_file")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DvcHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NocoBase anonymous signup then immediate myInAppChannels access (CVE-2026-52887 pre-exploit) AIDelivery Medium
Correlates a successful anonymous account creation via /api/auth:signUp (enabled by the default allowSignUp:true) with a request to the vulnerable /api/myInAppChannels:list resource from the same source IP within minutes. This is the article's stated exploitation prerequisite: sign up, sign in, then hit the loggedIn-ACL endpoint. Rationale: Chains the two article-named endpoints — /api/auth:signUp (default allowSignUp:true) and the vulnerable /api/myInAppChannels:list — on a shared source IP inside a 10-minute window, matching the documented signup→signin→exploit flow. Same-IP correlation strips ordinary user browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new-user onboarding where the account genuinely opens the in-app notifications panel
  • QA/automation account provisioning against a test instance
  • Load-testing or synthetic monitoring that signs up then exercises the API
  • Shared corporate egress IP where one user signs up and another (behind same NAT) opens notifications

| where DvcHostname !has "staging" and DvcHostname !has "test"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the myInAppChannels request query for SQLi tokens (UC1) — signup+access alone is suspicious, signup+injection is confirmed exploitation. 2) Contain: if the follow-on request carries injection, block the IP and disable auth-basic allowSignUp (POST-signup should require admin approval). 3) Hunt: enumerate all accounts created via /api/auth:signUp in the window and review their subsequent API activity for data exfil (COPY reads of the users table).

PostgreSQL backend spawning shell/LOLBin (COPY ... TO PROGRAM RCE, CVE-2026-52887) AIExploitation High
Detects the RCE tail of CVE-2026-52887: the PostgreSQL backend process (running as uid=999 postgres in the DB container) spawning a shell or command binary via COPY ... TO PROGRAM. A postgres process should never fork sh/bash/id/curl, so this parent→child pair is a near-certain indicator of stacked-statement SQLi execution. Rationale: Anchored on the article's confirmed RCE mechanics: COPY ... TO PROGRAM runs shell as uid=999(postgres). A postgres parent forking sh/bash/id/curl is behaviourally impossible in normal operation, giving a very low-FP endpoint signal that complements the web-layer UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/pull/9001
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Postgres archive_command / restore_command configured to call a shell script (WAL archiving)
  • PL/Perl or PL/Python stored procedures legitimately invoking helpers
  • DBA maintenance job using COPY TO PROGRAM for legitimate ETL/export
  • Container init or healthcheck script mis-parented under the postgres process tree
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "archive_command" and ProcessCommandLine !has "pg_wal"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — article shows payloads like 'id > /tmp/PWN_VERIFY.txt' and COPY reads of the users table; check the DB host /tmp for dropped files. 2) Contain: isolate the DB container, kill the spawned process tree, and rotate the exfiltrable secrets (users.password PBKDF2 hashes, admin id=1). 3) Hunt: correlate back to the originating web request (UC1) via timestamp, review any archive_command config to rule out benign use, and audit the postgres role for the rolsuper attribute that enabled COPY TO PROGRAM.

| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","cat","curl","wget","nc","ncat","chmod","python","python3","perl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

      AND (Filesystem.file_path="*/tmp/PWN_VERIFY.txt*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/tmp/PWN_HASH.txt*")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

OctLurk/LurkProxy/SilkLurk C2 beacon to campaign-specific domains & VPS IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint DNS resolutions and network connections to the hard-coded C2 domains and VPS IPs published for the OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy Central Asia campaign (e.g. dns.multitoconference.com, dns.ssentialserv.xyz connectivity check, 154.196.162.76). These indicators uniquely identify the campaign's command-and-control channel and are shared with the SilentRaid/MystRodX/TrustFall infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the campaign's hard-coded C2 domains (dns.multitoconference.com OctLurk beacon, dns.ssentialserv.xyz LurkProxy connectivity check) and the 11 VPS IPs, three of which Kaspersky/STS confirm overlap with SilentRaid/MystRodX/TrustFall infrastructure — high-fidelity, cross-sourced indicators. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/china-linked-uat-7290-targets-telecoms.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • digital.leroymerlin.com may collide with legitimate Leroy Merlin retail traffic on non-target networks — validate the resolved IP against the VPS list
  • Security appliances/sandboxes detonating samples and generating the same C2 lookups
  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS sinkhole services pre-resolving IOC domains
  • DNS logging proxies replaying historic queries during migration
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl == "digital.leroymerlin.com" and RemoteIP !in ("154.196.162.76","45.138.157.165","95.179.210.138","45.77.136.228","95.179.141.26","45.32.152.50","212.11.39.138","195.86.120.2","154.196.187.73","45.61.149.112","64.7.198.130"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName) that resolved/connected to the IOC and whether the host is a Central Asian government/ministry asset in scope. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the domain+IP at the firewall/DNS, and capture memory (both families run in-memory with a minimal on-disk loader). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the loader on disk, secretsdump/fscan/pp.txt activity, an AnyDesk-named keylogger, and lateral net-use to admin shares; sweep the fleet for any other IOC-list domain or IP.

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy/PlugX known sample hash execution or drop AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on process execution, image load, or file write matching the 16 MD5 hashes published for the OctLurk, SilkLurk, LurkProxy and side-loaded PlugX samples. Because both families are victim-specific and memory-resident, catching the minimal on-disk loader by hash is the cleanest execution-stage signal. Rationale: Directly uses the 16 published MD5s spanning OctLurk, SilkLurk, LurkProxy and side-loaded PlugX; hash IOCs are the highest-fidelity execution/install signal for memory-resident, victim-encoded loaders that otherwise leave minimal disk footprint. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysts detonating the samples in a monitored analysis VM
  • AV/EDR quarantine copies retaining the file and re-triggering file events
  • Threat-intel researchers storing IOC samples on a corporate share
  • Hash collision is effectively nil for MD5 at this scale but re-used loader stub across benign packers is theoretically possible
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\\Sandbox\\", @"\\Analysis\\", @"\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is on a production endpoint (not an analysis sandbox) and record host, user, path and initiating process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill/quarantine the sample, and capture volatile memory before reboot since the real payload lives in RAM. 3) Hunt: pull the loader's parent chain, look for the drive-serial/computer-name-keyed decode routine, and sweep for the C2 IOCs, secretsdump, fscan/pp.txt and AnyDesk-named keylogger across the estate.

Impacket secretsdump domain-controller hash extraction AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts command-line invocation of Impacket's secretsdump against domain controllers, matching the campaign's post-compromise step of harvesting password hashes from DCs. Anchors on secretsdump / -just-dc flags rather than LSASS access, so it complements existing credential-theft rules. Rationale: Article states hashes were harvested from domain controllers using Impacket's secretsdump.py; the secretsdump string plus -just-dc* flags are the tool's canonical invocation and rarely legitimate in production. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1003.006 T1003.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / purple-team exercises legitimately running Impacket
  • AD security assessments using secretsdump for auditing
  • A pentest tool named similarly living in a security team's toolkit share
  • Detection engineering validating this very rule with an atomic test
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\\RedTeam\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("PENTEST-01","SECAUDIT-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the source host/user is an authorized pentest asset; check the target (DC hostname) and whether -just-dc dumped NTDS. 2) Contain: disable the executing account, isolate the host, and treat all domain credentials as potentially compromised — begin krbtgt double-reset planning. 3) Hunt: correlate with the campaign C2 IOCs, look for prior remote-interactive logons to the DC, Pandora RC remote access, and subsequent lateral net-use to admin shares.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("secretsdump", "-just-dc-ntlm", "-just-dc-user", "-just-dc ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where CommandLine has_any ("secretsdump", "-just-dc-ntlm", "-just-dc-user", "-just-dc ")

AnyDesk-masquerading keylogger execution from non-standard path AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a process named like AnyDesk that is NOT the genuine signed AnyDesk binary, matching the campaign's keylogger that masquerades as AnyDesk to evade detection. Filters out the legitimate AnyDesk Software GmbH signed install. Rationale: Article states the keylogger 'masquerades as AnyDesk to sidestep detection'; matching an anydesk-named binary that lacks the AnyDesk Software GmbH signature and runs from a user-writable path isolates the impostor from genuine remote-support usage. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1056.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/unpacked AnyDesk run from Downloads by a legitimate support tech (usually still signed — the Company filter catches it)
  • Software-deployment staging AnyDesk to a ProgramData cache before install
  • Renamed legitimate AnyDesk copies by IT for allow-listing tests
  • Older AnyDesk builds with missing version metadata
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName) and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "AnyDesk"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the binary's signer/hash — a genuine AnyDesk is signed by 'AnyDesk Software GmbH'; an unsigned/mismatched one from a user path is the keylogger. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the file, and force-reset credentials typed on that host (keystrokes are captured). 3) Hunt: look for the parent loader, browser-password decryption of Chrome/Firefox, secretsdump, and outbound C2 to the campaign domains from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "anydesk"
| where not (FolderPath has @"\AnyDesk\" and (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "AnyDesk" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "AnyDesk"))
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "anydesk"
| where not (ActingProcessName has @"\AnyDesk\" and ActingProcessFileCompany has "AnyDesk")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fscan internal/public port scan using 'pp.txt' credential file AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts execution of Fscan-style network scanning that references the campaign's 'pp.txt' password file and targets SSH (22) and MySQL (3306), matching the described lateral-discovery step. Anchors on the specific pp.txt filename plus fscan/port artefacts for high fidelity. Rationale: Article names Fscan scanning SSH/22 and MySQL/3306 and using credentials from a password file 'pp.txt'; the literal pp.txt string and fscan binary are distinctive and unlikely to appear in benign admin activity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1046 T1110.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal vulnerability scans that happen to use fscan
  • A file literally named pp.txt used for unrelated benign purpose (rare in a cmdline arg)
  • Red-team engagement running fscan with a credential list
  • Network engineers troubleshooting SSH/MySQL reachability with a scripted scanner
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("VULNSCAN-01","PENTEST-01") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\\Nessus\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the scanning host is not an authorized scanner; review the fscan target ranges and whether pp.txt credentials succeeded against 22/3306. 2) Contain: isolate the host, rotate any credentials present in pp.txt, and review SSH/MySQL auth logs on scanned hosts for successful access. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host's C2 IOCs, secretsdump activity, and any resulting lateral net-use / Pandora RC remote sessions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pp.txt"
    or FileName has "fscan"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "fscan"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("-pwdf", "3306"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where CommandLine has "pp.txt" or CommandLine has "fscan" or NewProcessName endswith "\\fscan.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fscan Port Scan With pp.txt Credential File

SilkLurk collection: admin-share doc staging archived with WinRAR/7-Zip AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts WinRAR/7-Zip archiving spawned from cmd/PowerShell that follows connecting to network shares with admin credentials, matching SilkLurk's document-theft workflow (net use to admin shares → stage confidential docs → archive with WinRAR/7-Zip). Pairs the archiver child with a shell parent for fidelity. Rationale: Article describes SilkLurk using cmd→PowerShell to reach admin shares, stage confidential docs and archive them specifically with WinRAR and 7-Zip; the shell-parent + archiver-child + create/password flags combination isolates staging from interactive user archiving. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1039
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin backup scripts archiving directories with 7-Zip/WinRAR from a scheduled cmd/PowerShell task
  • Software packaging or log-bundling jobs creating password-protected archives
  • Helpdesk collecting diagnostic bundles via a PowerShell wrapper
  • Developers scripting release-artifact zips with rar.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Backup", "backup", "\\Scripts\\") and AccountName in~ ("svc-backup","backupadmin"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the archive command (source paths, output name, -hp password) and whether the parent shell recently ran net use to a C$/ADMIN$ share. 2) Contain: isolate the host, locate and preserve the archive before exfil, and block outbound to the campaign C2 IOCs. 3) Hunt: check for the preceding admin-share net use, SilkLurk DLL side-load/PlugX on the host, and any outbound transfer of the archive to non-corporate IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("rar.exe","winrar.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","7zg.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" a ", "-hp", " -p", "-r ", "a -r")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\rar.exe", "\\winrar.exe", "\\7z.exe", "\\7za.exe", "\\7zg.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe", "\\powershell.exe", "\\pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any (" a ", "-hp", " -p", "-r ", "a -r")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\PowerShell.exe) @Image:(*\rar.exe OR *\winrar.exe OR *\7z.exe OR *\7za.exe OR *\7zg.exe OR *\WinRAR.exe OR *\Rar.exe) @CommandLine:(*" a "* OR *-hp* OR *" -p"* OR *"-r "*)

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("rar.exe","winrar.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","7zg.exe") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process="* a *" OR Processes.process="*-hp*" OR Processes.process="* -p*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/

vault-secrets-webhook pod egress to cloud IMDS / external address (SSRF exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the outbound SSRF call itself: the vault-secrets-webhook process/pod connecting to the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) or any public IP, when it should only ever reach the internal Vault service. On EKS with IMDSv1 this hands the webhook pod's node/instance IAM identity to the attacker; more generally it is the wire-side confirmation that the annotation SSRF fired. Rationale: The webhook's only sanctioned destination is the internal Vault (https://vault:8200), so a connection from the vault-secrets-webhook process to IMDS 169.254.169.254 or any public IP is a direct wire-side signal of the SSRF the article describes; GuardDuty's IMDS/credential-exfil finding types corroborate the EKS IMDSv1 theft path the PoC calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/bank-vaults/vault-secrets-webhook/CVE-2026-54725/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1071.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate external Vault: org runs Vault as a SaaS/managed endpoint on a public IP, so webhook egress to that one public address is expected (allowlist it)
  • Node-level IMDS calls from the AWS SDK inside the webhook for legitimate cloud-auth (should target the internal Vault, not raw IMDS, but SDK credential lookups can hit IMDS)
  • Sidecar/service-mesh proxy sharing the pod network namespace attributed to the webhook process by node EDR
  • GuardDuty benign-positive IMDS findings from routine instance-profile credential retrieval on the node
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP != "203.0.113.10"   // replace with your approved external/managed Vault public IP(s) to suppress the one sanctioned destination
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the RemoteIP is not an approved external Vault; if it is 169.254.169.254 or an unknown public IP, correlate the timestamp with UC1 (malicious vault-addr admission) and UC2 (TokenRequest) on the same cluster. 2) Contain: network-policy the webhook pod to egress only the internal Vault service; if IMDS was reached on EKS, enforce IMDSv2 (hop limit 1) and rotate the node instance-profile credentials and any exposed SA tokens; upgrade to >=1.23.1. 3) Hunt: capture the destination and check whether it received an Authorization: Bearer JWT (proxy/Vault logs), then sweep other webhook-adjacent workloads for connections to the same external IP/domain.

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
